title: Apollo 13
description_block: EMBROIDERED MISSION PATCH FLOWN AROUND THE MOON. Commander James Lovell’s letter reads, in full:  “ The attached patch was flown aboard the Apollo 13 spacecraft on its flight round the moon April 11-17, 1970. / This patch was designed by the artist Lumen Winter after a mural he painted for the St. Regis Hotel in New York City. / Sincerely, / James A. Lovell. ”  The photograph included with the flown mission patch offers a view of the severely damaged Apollo 13 service module (SM) as captured from the lunar module/command module (CM). An entire panel on the SM was blown away by the explosion of an oxygen tank in the “Boom!” inscribed by LMP Fred Haise.

title: Apollo 13
description_block: FLOWN TO THE MOON ON APOLLO 13. At just under 56 hours into the Apollo 13 mission, an oxygen tank exploded when the cryogenic fans were activated, resulting in a major loss of electrical power to the Command and Service Module and forcing the crew to cancel the lunar landing. The present lot relates to the pressurization systems in the cabin of the Command Module Odyssey. The pressurization systems were integral to maintain and monitor to keep from further catastrophe, as the damage to the oxygen tank limited the breathable air available to the crew. The mission objective changed from the third attempted lunar landing to ensure the crew’s survival in the damaged spacecraft. The crew moved from the CSM Odyssey into the Lunar Module Aquarius, using it as a lifeboat for the four-day journey around the Moon and return to Earth. The NASA mission control staff and the contractor team worked around the clock to develop an alternate flight plan to return the crew to Earth safely despite seemingly insurmountable challenges. The mission stands out as a paragon of teamwork and first-class training.

title: Apollo 13
description_block: Apollo 13, meant to be the third mission to land humans on the moon, ran into trouble when damaged wire insulation ignited in an oxygen tank and vented the contents of both oxygen tanks in the Command Service Module Odyssey . The lunar landing was aborted and the mission objective became survival and successful return to Earth. The crew consisting of Commander James Lovell, Lunar Module Pilot Fred Haise, and Command Module Pilot Jack Swigert used the Lunar Module Aquarius as a lifeboat for their four day journey around the Moon and back to Earth. A successful burn of the Descent Stage put them on the proper trajectory back to Earth.  This burn was critical, as any error or another problem could cause a possible crash into the lunar surface.   The inscription by Fred Haise pointedly sums up their mission. While the Service Module explosion cancelled their lunar landing, the crew managed to safely maneuver their severely damaged spacecraft for a flight around the Moon and avoided any possible impact. An inadequately controlled engine burn or miscalculation could have sent them to a lunar impact. With people on the ground from both NASA and the contractor team working around the clock, an alternate flight plan was developed, and various procedures were developed to return the crew to Earth safely despite seemingly insurmountable challenges. The mission stands out as a paragon of teamwork and first-class training.

title: Apollo 13
description_block: FLOWN ON APOLLO 13 and SIGNED by TWO OF ITS CREW While the Apollo 13 crew never landed on the Moon in the Lunar Module Aquarius, the crew spent a great deal of time in the spacecraft and, as Fred Haise’s inscription references, it was crucial to their survival that they did not need to reference the LM Malfunctions Checklist. After the infamous explosion of an oxygen tank, the Apollo 13 crew had to move from the CSM Odyssey into the Lunar Module Aquarius, using it as a lifeboat in order to survive a four- day journey around the moon and return to Earth.  With people on the ground from both NASA and the contractor team working around the clock, an alternate flight plan was developed, and various procedures were developed to return the crew to Earth safely despite seemingly insurmountable challenges. The mission stands out as a paragon of teamwork and first-class training.

title: Apollo 13
description_block: CHEWING GUM FLOWN AROUND THE MOON ON APOLLO 13 Lunar Module Pilot Fred Haise’s letter reads in full:  “Displayed below is a ‘Chewing Gum’ packet that was carried around the moon on the flight of Apollo 13 during April 11 to 17, 1970. There are no labels on this particular gum packet.  Several food items were never eaten during the flight due to the oxygen tank explosion in Service Module which in turn caused an electrical power loss to the Command Module. That power loss eliminated the ability to supply and heat water for food rehydration. James Lovell, Jack Swigert, and myself mainly consumed the ‘wet pack’ type of foods during the Apollo 13 mission. Those foods did not require rehydration to eat. There were several gum packets onboard and this particular packet was not consumed.  This gum packet has been in my personal space artifact collection since 1970 which is now 35 years after the dramatic flight of Apollo 13. The flight was scheduled to be the third manned lunar landing mission, but those plans were aborted due to the above mentioned ‘problem.’ I have written ‘Flown around the moon on Apollo 13, Fred Hase, LMP’ on the front side of this packet.  Sincerely, Fred W. Haise / Apollo 13 Lunar Module Pilot.”

title: Apollo 13
description_block: A VIEW OF "THE LOST MOON" SIGNED AND EXTENSIVELY INSCRIBED BY CREW AND CAPCOM. Apollo 13, meant to be the third mission to land humans on the moon, ran into trouble when damaged wire insulation ignited in an oxygen tank and vented the contents of both oxygen tanks in the Command Service Module Odyssey . Though the crew made it safely back to Earth, the landing was canceled, and this view from their Lunar Module "lifeboat" during their lunar flyby is as close as the Apollo 13 astronauts got during the mission. They had precious few moments to observe the lunar surface up close before heading back to earth. The shut-down Command Module is visible out the overhead rendezvous window. The “PC+2 Burn” referenced in LMP Fred Haise’s inscription refers to the pericynthion + 2 burn. This burn was executed with the Descent Propulsion System of the Lunar Module Aquarius, an engine that was originally planned to help them land on the Moon. Approximately two hours after this photograph was taken on the crew's closest approach to the Moon, Haise completed a larger burn to shorten their return trip time by 10 hours. This maneuver saved them more electrical power, cooling water, and breathable oxygen to survive the voyage home.  CAPCOM Jack Lousma’s lengthy inscription also refers to their efforts to survive in the damaged spacecraft by moving to the Lunar Module Aquarius , which the crew treated  as a lifeboat.

title: Apollo 13
description_block: A RARE TEST STRIKE OF THE ORIGINAL APOLLO 13 ROBBINS MEDALLION WITH THE ORIGINAL CREW. The present lot is a lead test strike that was produced to gauge the quality of the impression before the final medallions were minted. This example for Apollo 13 is particularly interesting as its reverse has the initial design with Ken Mattingly, the original Command Module Pilot of the mission.  Mattingly was removed from the Apollo 13 crew after exposure to German Measles by backup LMP Charlie Duke. Mattingly was the only member of the prime crew who had no natural immunity to the disease and was replaced as CMP by Jack Swigert. In startling prescience, the mission emblem design visible on the obverse did not feature the crewmembers' names because the mission was broadly dedicated to the goal of advancing science for all humanity. Instead, it bears the phrase: "Ex-Luna Scientia," [From the Moon, Knowledge]. The fateful events of the mission underscored the staggering teamwork of hundreds of engineers on Earth to assist the crew in returning home. Aside from the Apollo 11 emblem, which similarly left off crew names as the mission was dedicated for all humankind, all other Apollo emblems feature the names of the astronauts involved. This design feature meant that the medal’s reverse is the only location on the medal in which the crew members were listed and Mattingly’s original crew placement was referenced. After the mission, all 404 flown Robbins Medals were restruck to bear the corrected crew names.

title: Apollo 13
description_block: SIGNED on the front of the cover by JAMES LOVELL, FRED HAISE, and KEN MATTINGLY, the original Command Module Pilot of Apollo 13, who was grounded before the launch due to his exposure to rubella.   Since astronauts were unable to obtain adequate life insurance due to the high-risk nature of their missions, each crew signed a group of covers and evenly distributed them among their families for safe keeping prior to each mission. If an unfortunate event prevented the crew’s safe return, the covers would have provided a limited financial means of support to their families on Earth. Due to the infamous explosion of a cryogenic oxygen tank on their way to the Moon, the Apollo 13 crew’s families almost had to use their insurance covers.   Chuck Friedlander served as Chief at the NASA Astronaut Support Office, KSC from 1963-1967, leaving shortly after the Apollo 1 tragedy for CBS News where he was Walter Cronkite’s Space Technical Consultant from 1967-1969. Apollo 8 astronaut William Anders invited Friedlander to join him in Washington as his Executive Assistant when he served as Executive Secretary of the National Aeronautics and Space Council (NASC) at the White House, from 1969-1972. Friedlander also served as Vice President of the Board of Directors for the International Aerospace Hall of Fame, San Diego, CA from 1973-1980.

title: Apollo 9
description_block: A Group of Manuals and Assorted Mission Documents used by Stuart “Stu” Roosa as a member of the Apollo 9 Astronaut Support Crew, including his mission-critical CAPCOM notebook. Apollo 14 Command Module Pilot Stu Roosa and his Apollo 14 crew mate Ed Mitchell both served as members of the Apollo 9 astronaut support crew. Apollo 9 was a wildly ambitious mission from a technical and engineering standpoint, as its success determined whether a Moon landing was possible- in JFK’s stated timeframe or otherwise.  Roosa’s original assignment was to assist in coordinating the activities in mission control during Apollo 9. To prepare for the assignment, Roosa studied the technical details of the mission and logged months and months of simulation with the flight controllers. This training and expertise proved incredibly valuable when Rusty Schweickart, Apollo 9’s Lunar Module Pilot, grew ill on the flight due to motion sickness. Roosa was integral in reorganizing the schedule to salvage as many mission objectives as possible.  As historian Andrew Chaikin writes in his Apollo Program chronology, Man on the Moon, “ [Roosa] knew more about the flight plan than any astronaut who was still on earth, and he was at the Capcom’s mike almost every minute that McDivitt’s crew was awake” (p. 345).  The incredible depth of Roosa’s expertise and collaborative spirit to help the crew of Apollo 9 through their mission are showcased not only in his CapCom notebook with pages of notes and calculations but in a certificate awarded him for his support “in the trenches.”  Altogether, the manuals, notebooks, assorted documents, and certificate in the present lot speak to the staggering technical expertise required to make humanity’s first steps on the Moon.  Roosa’s exemplary performance on the Apollo 9 mission drew the attention of Deke Slayton and Chris Kraft as they planned the crews for the later Apollo missions. His assistance to the Apollo 9 crew helped lead to his placement of the prime crew of Apollo 14 without having served as a backup.

title: Apollo 11
description_block: A FAMOUS IMAGE OF THE HISTORIC LUNAR LANDING, SIGNED AND INSCRIBED BY THE APOLLO 11 CREW TO APOLLO 14 COMMAND MODULE PILOT STU ROOSA WITH THANKS FOR MAKING IT POSSIBLE. Stuart Roosa was among the “Original 19,” NASA Astronaut Group 5, along with other Apollo astronauts such as Charlie Duke, Fred Haise, Jack Swigert and Edgar Mitchell. Roosa was assigned to cover the Saturn boosters along with Charlie Duke, which initially seemed unimportant, until the Apollo missions neared. He served as CAPCOM at the Launch Complex 34 blockhouse during the Apollo 1 tragedy on January 27, 1967, but it was his performance supporting mission control on Apollo 9 that earned him the respect of his fellow astronauts – and most importantly, the notice of Chief of the Astronaut Office Alan Shepard. Roosa had been assigned to the mission because of his diligence with the Saturn boosters. He showed the same diligence training for Apollo 9 and spent months in simulations with the flight controllers. When Lunar Module Pilot Rusty Schweickart began to suffer from space adaptation syndrome (space sickness) on the first day in orbit, Roosa, who knew the flight plan better than nearly everyone else, helped to reorganize the mission schedule and save as many of the objectives as possible. He was at the CAPCOM mike nearly the entire time that the crew was awake. Roosa's quick thinking kept the Apollo 11 mission on schedule as well. It was a key contribution to making Armstrong, Aldrin, and Collins' historic lunar landing happen within the deadline set by John F. Kennedy to get boots on the Moon by the end of the decade. The now-iconic image of Lunar Module Pilot Buzz Aldrin walking on the lunar surface during the Apollo 11 EVA was captured by Mission Commander Neil Armstrong (seen in the reflection of Buzz's visor) as they explored the Sea of Tranquility. One of the most famous images in modern history, the present lot is additionally signed with a heartfelt message of thanks to Stu Roosa directly from Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins. It's a reminder of the respect Roosa's diligence and expertise earned in the astronaut corps. This respect would later earn him a spot on the Apollo 14 prime crew as Command Module Pilot without ever having served as backup.

title: Apollo 14
description_block: APOLLO 14 MANUALS AND POSTFLIGHT DOCUMENTS USED BY COMMAND MODULE PILOT STUART ROOSA Altogether, the manuals and assorted documents with notes and annotations in the present lot speak to the staggering technical expertise required for an Apollo mission to the Moon.  Postponed due to the near-disaster that was Apollo 13, Apollo 14 was humanity’s third trip to the lunar surface. Commander Alan Shepard, Command Module Pilot Stuart Roosa, and Lunar Module Pilot Edgar Mitchell were originally assigned Apollo 13, before Dr. George Mueller swapped the Apollo 13 and Apollo 14 crews in order to give Alan Shepard more time to train once he was returned to flight status. The resultant delay in their mission, especially after the events of Apollo 13, meant that the Apollo 14 crew trained for a total of nineteen months and logged more time than any Apollo crew before them.  The Command and Service Module (CSM) had to undergo changes after the Apollo 13 investigation. These were supervised by Roosa. The thorough care with which they approached their training and these changes is apparent in the handwritten notes in several margins of documents in this lot, particularly in Command Module schematics. Apollo 14 almost ended in a mission failure as well. Early in the mission, there was a technical failure that prevented the Lunar Module Antares and the Command Module Kitty Hawk from connecting. On the ground prior to the mission, Roosa had gone through mission simulations of the required maneuvers so many times that he was on track to break the record for using less fuel than any Command Module Pilot before him. He would have broken the record if not for a faulty docking latch that kept the two spacecraft from engaging. After five attempts and troubleshooting in collaboration with mission control and the astronaut support crew led by Gene Cernan, Roosa successfully docked on the sixth attempt and continued their mission.  Apollo 13’s aborted Moon landing mission also meant that the scientific objectives assigned to that mission were then inherited by Apollo 14. Shepherd and Mitchell, in the Lunar Module Antares , landed in the Fra Mauro region of the highlands originally assigned to Apollo 13’s Aquarius. In the Command Module Kitty Hawk , one of Roosa’s roles was to survey the lunar surface from orbit for future missions by taking hi-res photos with a Hycon camera, a handheld topographic camera based on models used in reconnaissance satellites at the time. To be best equipped for this responsibility, Roosa also spent time training with geologist Farouk El-Baz. He trained by running simulations in his Northrop T-38 jet and observing at a similar speed and altitude. The Hycon malfunctioned after approximately 140 frames, which led Roosa to have to take detailed photographs of the Descartes highlands (the proposed landing site for the upcoming Apollo 16 mission) with a Hasselblad camera while ensuring that the Kitty Hawk was angled precisely to take each shot as it sped past (Chaikin, p 365). The Apollo 14 lunar maps and landmarks documents in this lot have annotations speaking to this experience. Each of the documents in this lot speak to the massive scope of technical details that required total mastery to ensure mission success. After the “successful failure” of Apollo 13, NASA could not afford another failure of any kind. The astronauts and support personnel trained extensively through the use of these documents to ensure mission success and the continuation of the Apollo program.  REFERENCES Chaikin, Andrew. A Man on the Moon: The Voyages of the Apollo Astronauts. 2019 Penguin Random House, London.

title: Apollo 14
description_block: SPACE FOOD FROM THE COLLECTION OF APOLLO 14 CMP STUART ROOSA Apollo 14 astronauts had both dehydrated, cubed foods and freeze-dehydrated foods. The cubed foods, like the bacon bars in the present lot, were solid foods compressed, dehydrated, and vacuum-packed in plastic. These solid foods were then rehydrated by the astronauts’ saliva as they chewed.  All food and beverage packs for each astronaut were stored in aluminum packages that were then color coded for specific crew at specific meals. Red velcro indicated it was meant for mission commander Alan Shepard, blue velcro indicated food for Lunar Module Pilot Ed Mitchell, and white velcro for Command Module Pilot Stu Roosa. The Apollo 14 astronauts’ menu released by NASA featured bacon squares as a breakfast item for Roosa as a part of Meal C on 3 and 5 of the mission. Pantry Stowage documents list 12 total packs of bacon bites included in the astronauts’ pantry from days 6 through 10 of the mission.   Lunar flown food is rare as it was made to be consumed or disposed of on the mission itself.  REFERENCES Apollo 14 Crew Menus enclosed “Memorandum to DC/Chief, Preventive Medicine Division from DC71/Food and Nutrition. Subject: Apollo 14 GFE FRR Preboard,” 8 Dec 1970. NASA Manned Spacecraft Center, Houston, Texas.

title: Apollo 14
description_block: [Apollo 14] USS New Orleans Recovery Caps and Plaque Presented to Command Module Pilot Stuart Roosa Two wool USS New Orleans Recovery Caps presented to Apollo 14 Command Module Pilot Stuart Roosa, one personalized with his name embroidered (spelled incorrectly, “Stewart A. Roosa”) in gold thread on the back. Both hats are made of wool, size 7 ¼ and nonadjustable. The additional hat without personalized embroidery has “ROOSA” inscribed on the interior tag in black ink.  TOGETHER WITH: one wooden and brass plaque bearing the insignia of the USS New Orleans LPH-11 (designating the ship as an amphibious assault ship, LPH refers to “Landing Platform Helicopter”). Plaque measures 8 x 10 inches. The plaque is inscribed "ASTRONAUT STUART A. ROOSA / 'APOLLO 14.'" ACCOMPANIED BY: a personalized, Apollo 14 commemorative zippo lighter in original box with warranty pamphlet. .

title: Apollo 14
description_block: The Mercury 7 began the tradition of astronauts wearing a lapel pin with the design of a three-tailed shooting star encircled by an ellipse. Astronaut candidates and trained astronauts wore silver pins in that design until their first spaceflight, and astronauts who had flown in space wore a gold version. Notably, the Apollo 14 crew included Alan Shepard, one of the original Mercury astronauts. As a result, the mission emblem for Apollo 14 was the first to include the three-tailed shooting star, although this later became a commonly-used element in mission emblem designs.  This beautiful lithographic poster features the golden three-tailed star approaching the Moon after launching from Earth, illustrating the path taken by the three crew members Alan Shepard, Stuart “Stu” Roosa, and Edgar Mitchell.

title: Apollo 14
description_block: TWO APOLLO ERA FLIGHT SUITS AND JACKET RELATING TO THE APOLLO 14 MISSION AND PANAMA JUNGLE SURVIVAL TRAINING While NASA missions were planned to end with a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean rather than on land, Apollo astronauts were trained on how to survive and navigate jungle terrain in case they landed off-course on their return from space. The present lot includes materials astronauts trained with as well as photographs of this Panama jungle survival school taken in June 1967. The astronauts spent three days in Panama learning how to survive in the jungle, divided into three-man crews and only provided with the materials included in the onboard survival kit. Apollo 14 Command Module Pilot Stuart "Stu" Roosa was no stranger to wilderness survival due to his training as a smokejumper in the United States Forest Service. Smokejumpers are firefighters trained to jump from airplanes to extinguish isolated forest fires. Roosa jumped in crews putting out fires in Oregon and California in the summer of 1953. This experience proved to be an asset to Roosa in his illustrious career as a pilot and later as an Apollo astronaut.  Roosa would have worn the gold suit and jacket in his flights training for the Apollo 14 mission and when training as backup CMP for Apollo 16 and 17. He would have been in line to command Apollo 20 if the program hadn’t prematurely ended.  This lot is accompanied by several photographs that offer a unique look at astronaut training, both in jungle survival and in testing the launch abort astronaut evacuation system.

title: Apollo 16
description_block: APOLLO ASTRONAUT STUART ROOSA'S BACKUP CREW PATCHES FOR APOLLO 16, COMPLETE WITH MISSION REPORT. Stuart Roosa was known for his thorough technical expertise, so much so that he was hand picked by Apollo 14 Commander Alan Shepard to be a member of the Apollo 14 prime crew before serving on the backup crew of an Apollo mission. Roosa first served as a member of the astronaut support crew for Apollo 9, an especially ambitious mission laying the groundwork for the future lunar landing. When the Apollo 9 Lunar Module Pilot Rusty Schweickart fell ill due to space sickness, no one on Earth at the time knew the mission's flight plan as well as Roosa. He had spent months in simulations with the flight controllers prior to launch, and used that expertise to help reorganize the mission schedule and save as many of the objectives as possible to keep the future Moon missions on schedule. He was at the CAPCOM mike nearly the entire time that the crew was awake. His diligence caught the attention of Al Shepard, who had just been cleared for flight after undergoing a newly developed surgery that cured the Ménière's disease that had kept him grounded since his legendary Mercury flight. One of Shepard's last acts as Chief of the Astronaut Office was picking his crew for the mission he would command. He chose for prime crew Stu Roosa as Command Module Pilot (CMP) and Edgar Mitchell as Lunar Module Pilot (LMP). It was unprecedented for an astronaut to be selected for an Apollo prime crew without having flown or served as backup crew for a previous mission, which caused a stir among other astronauts that Shepard was quick to quash. The patches in the present lot are from the first time Roosa served as backup, a unique departure from the typical trajectory of Apollo astronauts. If Roosa had flown on Apollo 16 or 17 as CMP, there is a chance he could have broken the record for most efficient docking, as he would have broken the record during Apollo 14 if not for a faulty latch mechanism. Prior to Apollo 14, Roosa had trained through 19 months of mission simulations, more than any other Apollo CMP, and he was track to break the record for using less fuel than any Command Module Pilot before him if the docking hatch had fully functioned. Roosa served as backup CMP for Apollo 16 and 17 and would have been in line to command Apollo 20 if the program hadn’t prematurely ended.

title: Apollo 14
description_block: LUNAR SURFACE FLOWN MISSION PATCH DESIGNED AND PLACED BY THE APOLLO 14 BACKUP CREW IN THE LUNAR MODULE ANTARES Stafford’s letter printed on his USAF Flag Rank stationery reads in full: “This BEEP BEEP patch was carried on the flight of Apollo 14 during January 31 to February 9, 1971 and was one of the ‘gotcha’ patches in Lunar Module Antares.  It stayed some 33 hours on the Moon inside Antares during February 5 and 6. It was given to me by Apollo 14 Commander Alan Shepard after the flight.  Full details of this unusual patch are provided in my SBH letterhead background summary.” Lt. General Stafford’s Stafford, Burke and Hecker (SBH) letter reads, in part : “This patch was personalized by the Apollo 14 back-up crew of Gene Cernan, Ron Evans and Joe Engle.  They are the only Apollo back-up crew to have their own mission patch. The design stems from the fact of Alan Shepard returned to active space flight status after years being grounded since 1963 due to Meniere’s disease, an inner-ear ailment.  Shepard had this condition surgically corrected in 1968 and was selected to command Apollo 14. He was the oldest astronaut to fly any Apollo mission. In Gene’s 1999 book, ‘The Last Man on the Moon,’ he describes the good-natured ribbing by his back-up crew to Shepard’s crew: ‘Ron, Joe and I called ourselves the First Team, to infer that we were better than they were.  I was always giving Al mock warnings not to mess up, because the First Team was standing right there, ready to strap in and fly that Saturn V if the old man (and his crew) couldn’t hack it.’ This patch ‘was a gotcha on Al, for it depicted a gray-bearded Wile E. Coyote (Shepard’s crew) coming up from the Earth only to find a “First Team” Roadrunner already standing on the Moon, chirping his famous “Beep-Beep! Every time we would give him a “Beep-Beep” jab, Shepard would shoot right back, “Beep, beep, your ass!” “All the way to the Moon and back, even on the lunar surface, whenever the crew opened a box, bag or locker, out would float a First Team mission patch.  Ron, Joe and I, as the backup crew, had final access to the spacecraft, and while we set switches and checked the gauges, we also stuffed our Roadrunner patches into every nook and cranny, setting up a future mini-blizzard of gotchas… On the private radio loop during the flight of Apollo 14 was Shepard’s annoyance when still another patch would suddenly appear.  “Tell Cernan,” he growled, “Beep-Beep, his ass.”’ This patch was given to me after the Apollo 14 flight by Alan Shepard as a thank-you for my work while I was Chief of the Astronaut Office, Manned Spacecraft Center, Houston, Texas in 1971.  It is one of the lunar surface patches that continued to annoy Al while he and Edgar Mitchell explored the lunar surface during February 5 and 6, 1971.  It spent some 33 hours on lunar surface during the Apollo 14 flight which began on January 31 and returned to earth on February 9, 1971. THOMAS P. STAFFORD, LT. GENERAL, USAF (Ret.), Gemini 6 Pilot (1965) and Gemini 9 Commander (1966), Apollo 10 Commander (1969) Apollo Commander, Apollo Soyuz (1975)” Apollo 14 “First Team” patches are rare and seldom seen on the market.

title: Apollo 14
description_block: A PHOTOGRAPH FROM THE LONGEST MOONWALK OF THE APOLLO PROGRAM. Apollo 14 Commander Alan Shepard and Lunar Module Pilot (LMP) Ed Mitchell spent a total of nine hours navigating the Lunar Surface. 4 hours and 34 minutes were dedicated to their extravehicular activity (EVA) to Cone Crater, which took longer than expected due to inconsistencies between their maps and the terrain before them. This made their EVA the longest moonwalk in history. As alluded to in the inscription, this striking image captures Mitchell, the sixth person to walk on the Moon, in the search for Cone Crater. Cone Crater is a geological formation created by an asteroid impact encompassing the 1100 kilometer Imbrium basin, the second largest impact basin on the Moon. Shepard and Mitchell’s mission objectives were to collect samples of crater ejecta in order to help determine the temperature, pressure, and time of the Imbrium impact. Unbeknownst to the Commander and LMP, they were only 135 feet away from the crater when they decided to turn back. They still successfully completed their mission, collecting samples that were able to determine the Imbrium impact’s occurrence at approximately 3.93 billion years ago.  NASA’s Apollo 14 Lunar Surface Journal transcribes Mitchell’s conversation with CAPCOM Fred Haise (also the Apollo 13 LMP) as they search for Cone Crater: “It's going to take longer than we expected. Our positions are all in doubt now, Freddo” (NASA, 133:06:22 ).

title: Apollo 15
description_block: LET THERE BE LIGHT. The present lot was flown in the Lunar Module Falcon , which landed on the lunar surface July 30, 1971. It provided additional light as needed to Commander Dave Scott inside the LM from their landing site in the Hadley-Apennine region. Hadley Rille, close to the Apennine Mountains, was chosen in part for the variety of its terrain. The rough terrain made for a hard landing, but the imagery of the gentle mountains behind the astronauts seen in the increased television coverage and excellent surface photography helped to revive public interest in the Apollo program. The Apollo 15 mission illuminated our understanding of science in multiple ways. Most notably, Dave Scott demonstrated Galileo’s theory that objects of differing mass, in this case a hammer and a feather, fall at the same rate when air resistance isn’t a factor. The present lot is a rare example of lunar module flight-used hardware originating from the personal collection of a Moonwalker who used it.

title: Apollo 15
description_block: In a photo taken on August 1, 1971, Mission Commander Dave Scott gives a military salute while standing beside the United States flag, which had been deployed near the end of Scott and Irwin's second EVA. The present view looks due south, with Hadley Delta in the background rising approximately 13,124 feet above the plain. Also of scientific note: during his time on the lunar surface, Scott used a hammer and a feather to validate Galileo's theory that—without air resistance—objects will fall at the same rate, regardless of their mass.

title: Apollo 16
description_block: The famous image of Commander John Young doing his jumping American flag salute with the lunar lander and rover in the background. Young completed three EVAs in the Descartes Highlands with Lunar Module Pilot Charles Duke, making him the ninth person to walk on the moon.

title: Apollo 16
description_block: This incredible image shows Duke on the lunar surface (EVA-1 at Plum Crater) during the penultimate Apollo mission. When the 36 year old astronaut descended from the Lunar Module into the Descartes Highlands, he became the tenth and youngest person to walk on the Moon, prompting him to exclaim: "Fantastic! Oh, that first foot on the lunar surface is super, Tony!" ﻿

title: Apollo 17
description_block: LUNAR SURFACE FLOWN APOLLO 17 MISSION EMBLEM, PRESENTED BY THE LAST MOONWALKER TO A FELLOW ASTRONAUT Thomas P. Stafford’s Typed Letter Signed reads: “This crew emblem was carried on the flight of Apollo 17 during December 7 to 19, 1972. It was taken to the lunar surface and stayed some 75 hours inside Lunar Module Challenger between December 11 and 14, 1972. It was given to me by Apollo 17 Commander Gene Cernan after the flight. Gene was my LMP on the Apollo 10 flight I commanded during May 1969.”

title: Apollo 17
description_block: APOLLO 17 BETA CLOTH EMBLEM FLOWN TO THE MOON, SIGNED BY THE LAST MAN TO WALK ON THE MOON The iconic "Blue Marble" photograph of the Earth, taken on 7 December 1972 from CSM America . The image was captured by the crew whilst en route to the Moon, and at a distance of about 18,000 miles. Africa, Antarctica, and the Arabian Peninsula are visible in this image. This beta cloth emblem was flown in the Command Module "America" on the final Apollo mission to the Moon.

title: Apollo 17
description_block: LMP Harrison Schmitt stands next to the deployed United States flag during an EVA at the Taurus-Littrow landing site. In this remarkable photograph taken by Commander Gene Cernan, the top of the flag seems to point toward Earth. Trained as a geologist, Schmitt was the first and only professional scientist to walk on the Moon. Apollo 17 was the last of the Apollo missions, making Harrison Schmitt and Gene Cernan the last Moonwalkers.

title: Apollo 17
description_block: Apollo 17 launched on December 7, 1972, with Gene Cernan as its commander. Before reentering the LM for the final time, Gene Cernan expressed his thoughts thus: "as I take man's last step from the surface, back home for some time to come...I'd like to just [say] what I believe history will record. That America's challenge of today has forged man's destiny of tomorrow. And, as we leave the Moon at Taurus-Littrow, we leave as we came and, God willing, as we shall return, with peace and hope for all mankind." His sentiments are captured in his inscription on the present photograph.  Apollo 17 was the last and the longest chapter of the Apollo program, lasting a total of 12 days and 14 hours, with 75 hours spent on the lunar surface. The mission garnered a number of record-setting achievements. These included three EVAs totaling about 22 hours of exploration of the Taurus-Littrow valley. Mission Commander Cernan and Lunar Module Pilot Schmitt covered that 22 miles using the Lunar Rover and collected a record 75 pounds of geologic samples. Cernan piloted the Rover on its final run, during which he clocked a maximum speed of 11.2 mph, giving him the (unofficial) lunar land speed record.   As Cernan boarded the LM Challenger, he became the last man to walk on the Moon.

title: Apollo, Skylab
description_block: A GROUP OF EARLY TEST STRIKES OF ROBBINS MEDALLIONS FROM APOLLO AND SKYLAB MISSIONS The present lot offers an unusual glimpse at the creation process of Robbins medallions. Robbins Medallions were commemorative medallions minted in both silver and gold by the Robbins Company. They were produced expressly to be flown as mementos, starting with Apollo 7 and running through the Shuttle programs. The medallions were only available to be purchased by the astronauts, and for some missions, there were more medals minted than flown. The present lot is a group of lead test strikes produced to gauge the quality of the impression before the medallions were minted.

title: Apollo Program
description_block: A MASSIVE PICTORIAL HISTORY OF THE APOLLO PROGRAM, COMPILED FOR "THE MAN WHO PUT MEN ON THE MOON." The over one thousand photographs, including many NASA "red number" examples, compiled across twelve volumes offer a comprehensive, behind-the-scenes look at one of the most celebrated achievements in human history. Hailed as “The Man who put Men on the Moon” and the “Father of the Manned Spacecraft Program,” Dr. George Mueller played a pivotal role at NASA from 1963-1969. He was originally sworn in as Deputy Associate Administrator for Manned Space Flight on September 1, 1963, but his title quickly changed to Associate Administrator for Manned Space Flight after an internal reorganization and he remained in that role until he left NASA in December 1969. Several photographs in this lot capture key moments in Mueller's career, from his official swearing in to his visits to global tracking stations and shots of his work in Mission Control. Mueller led the Office of Manned Spaceflight at NASA Headquarters, what is now the Human Operations and Exploration Mission Directorate. In this role, he shaped all operations leading to the fulfillment of President Kennedy’s ambitious goal of a lunar landing by the end of the decade. Renowned pioneer of spaceflight Dr. Werner Von Braun commented, “Without George Mueller, we would not have landed on the moon as soon as we did.” Mueller set and managed the schedule for the entire program and ensured that the costs of landing men on the Moon, when accounting for inflation, were exactly the same as projected at the outset of the program six years before. A former professor before his tenure as deputy administrator, Mueller did not believe in asking others to execute tasks he would not be willing to do himself. Before the first extravehicular activities (EVAs) took place in space by Gemini astronauts, Mueller himself flew in a KC-135 zero gravity aircraft in a pressurized space suit, personally verifying that he could get into and out of the space craft in zero gravity. There are several photographs of Mueller suited up in NASA's early water testing from this period, as well as images of other key players in the race to put Americans on the Moon. In addition to beautiful "red number" photographs known to collectors, such as the iconic Apollo 8 Earthrise, this lot features hundred of photos of vehicle testing, launches, and crew recoveries.

title: Apollo Program
description_block: THE EARTH AS SEEN BY APOLLO ASTRONAUTS A beautiful photo of Earth as seen from space, signed by several Apollo Astronauts and Moonwalkers, including Buzz Aldrin, Dave Scott, Charlie Duke, and Frank Borman.

title: Apollo Program
description_block: A PHOTOGRAPHIC ARCHIVE OF THE FIRST AND LAST CREWED APOLLO FLIGHTS Just under one hundred images in the present lot illustrate the incredible milestones achieved by Apollo 7, Apollo 8, 15, 16, and 17. Apollo 7 was the first crewed flight of the Apollo program. Commander Walter M. Schirra, Command Module Pilot Donn F. Eisele, and Lunar Module Pilot R. Walter Cunningham tested the newly redesigned Command and Service Modules in space after the Apollo 1 tragedy. Apollo 8 was humanity's first journey to the Moon, crewed by Frank Borman, William Anders, and Jim Lovell. A striking Earthrise from this mission is included in the lot. Apollo 15 was the fourth landing on the Moon, and the first with the iconic lunar rover or "Moon Buggy." The Moon Buggy grew more advanced each mission, ensuring Apollo 16 and 17 covered astonishing ground with each crewed landing to the Moon. Apollo 17 was the last of the Apollo missions and the last time humans walked on the Moon. This archive features photographs from that mission and fittingly ends with the recovery of Apollo 17's crew Commander Gene Cernan, Lunar Module Pilot Harrison Schmitt, and Command Module Pilot Ronald E. Evans from the Pacific after they splashed down in their capsule America.

title: From The Earth to the Moon
description_block: SIGNED BY 10 ASTRONAUTS, INCLUDING 5 MOONWALKERS. Neil Armstrong mentioned  From the Earth to the Moon  during a television broadcast from the Apollo 11 spacecraft on July 23, 1969, the day before he and his crew mates returned to Earth. " A hundred years ago, Jules Verne wrote a book about a voyage to the Moon. His spaceship, Columbia  [sic],  took off from Florida and landed in the Pacific Ocean after completing a trip to the Moon. It seems appropriate to us to share with you some of the reflections of the crew as the modern-day Columbia completes its rendezvous with the planet Earth and the same Pacific Ocean tomorrow." With signatures from Apollo 11 Lunar Module Pilot (LMP) Buzz Aldrin and Apollo 17 Commander (CDR) Gene Cernan, the present lot is signed by crews from the first and last missions to walk on the Moon.

title: Moonwalkers
description_block: One of the largest lunar maps ever produced for NASA during the Apollo program. All large craters and mare are labeled including unique features such as rilles and ejecta rays. These features are based on image data from all five Lunar Orbiter Spacecraft.

title: Skylab
description_block: An early model of Skylab, America's first space station, originally from the collection of the father of the program. The 1/100 scale model was created by Bendix's Navigation and Control Division, responsible for the Skylab Apollo Telescope Mount (ATM). Skylab was America’s first (and only exclusively operated) space station. It was constructed from a repurposed Saturn V third stage (the S-IVB), and took the place of that stage during launch. Fitted with an orbital workshop, a solar observatory, and several hundred life science and physical science experiments, it was incredibly productive over its brief life. Skylab's contributions to science and the development of human life in space are especially remarkable considering the damage sustained during its launch when the micrometeoroid shield was torn off and the debris jammed one of the large solar array panels, tearing another panel off completely. The first crew, Commander Pete Conrad, Pilot Paul Weitz and Science Pilot Joe Kerwin as part of Skylab 2 were tasked with repairing the space station, which they did on the first-ever repair spacewalk. The crew were still able, during their month-long stay, to complete much of the planned scientific research, their primary goal.  Alan Bean, Owen Garriot, and Jack Lousma served as the Skylab III crew. Their flight time totaled 59 days and 11 hours, more than double the record set by Skylab II. The crew implemented improvements and insights learned from Skylab II, accomplishing three hundred hours more research than initially planned and returning to Earth in better health than the prior crew had.   Together, the Skylab missions capped off NASA’s first fifteen years as an agency and served as a significant and often undersung chapter of human life in space. The present model is an early conception of Skylab which, curiously, includes a docked Lunar Module, which wasn't used on any of the Skylab mission.

title: Apollo, Skylab
description_block: EXTENSIVE CHRONOLOGY OF SPACECRAFT FROM APOLLO TO SKYLAB, SIGNED BY A MEMBER OF EVERY CREWED APOLLO FLIGHT AND THE COMMANDERS OF EACH SKYLAB MISSION - SIGNED BY 8 MOONWALKERS A complete set of the hardcover, NASA-issued The Apollo Spacecraft: A Chronology is a rare find, made more so by the several signatures of astronauts who took the Apollo spacecraft to the Moon. In addition to the complete Apollo spacecraft chronologies, this library includes authoritative texts relating to SKYLAB and the APOLLO-SOYUZ TEST PROJECT. Skylab, America's first space station, fulfilled the dream of Wernher von Braun to build an orbiting station where people could live and work in space for extended periods. The Orbital Workshop (OWS), the largest component of Skylab, was built according to Von Braun and his team's brilliant idea of using a spent S-IVB rocket stage. There were two approaches for getting the workshop into orbit; first was known as the "wet" workshop, consisting of a multiple docking adapter, which permitted up to five spacecraft to be docked to Workshop at once; an airlock module attached to the OWS; and Crew quarters in the S-IVB hydrogen tank, with two wings covered with solar cells. These components would all be added after the crew had docked with the station in space, replaced all of the residual propellants from the S-IVB stage with breathable oxygen, before outfitting the tank as a space station. Another simpler method, known as the "dry" workshop, involved launching a fully outfitted Workshop — this approach was not used because all Saturn V launch vehicles were already earmarked for the Apollo programs, and thus the more complicated "wet" approach had to be used.  The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) signaled the symbolic end of the Space Race that started with the launch of Sputnik in 1957. It was the first joint US-Soviet space flight, during which the US Apollo Command/Service Module docked with the Soviet Soyuz 19 capsule, and the two crews: US astronauts Tom Stafford, Vance Brand, and Deke Slayton; and Russian Cosmonauts Alexey Leonov and Valeri Kubasov, visited each other’s ships, shared meals, and conducted experiments together. ASTP was the last crewed US space mission until the first Space Shuttle flight in 1981. The Cosmonauts have signed their names and inscribed in English “V. Kubasov” and “Leonov.”

title: Mars Globe
description_block: FIRST EDITION of this large, visual relief globe created using data acquired by the Mariner 9 probe, launched on May 30, 1971 and sent back to the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, National Aeronautics and Space Administration in Pasadena, Ca. The remarkable images returned by Mariner 9 revealed an incredibly rocky landscape reminiscent of the lunar surface. After completing its final transmission on October 27, 1972, Mariner 9 had returned 7,329 photos and mapped 85% of the Red Planet.

title: Viking Lander
description_block: The Viking program was a NASA Langley Research Center-managed project whose objective was to study the atmosphere and surface of Mars, obtain high-resolution imagery and to search for evidence of life. The program sent two space probes, each composed of two sections: an orbiter and a lander, each launched by Titan IIIE rockets with Centaur upper stages. The contract for the lander went to Martin Marietta of Denver, CO, who was also responsible for the launch system. Marietta labels are visible on the flight case included with the lot. The landing site for each mission was chosen by astronomer Carl Sagan.  This spare of the Surface Sampler Acquisition Assembly, which would be fitted with sampler boom and a soil sampler head, was one of the key components of the Viking Lander. In practice, the sampler boom extends from the housing assembly pushing the sampler head to the Martian surface to take a scoop of soil. The soil is deposited into a receptacle on the Lander which routes the sample to three scientific experiments: biological, gas chromatograph/mass spectrometer and water analysis. The information collected during the two Viking missions provided data that helped to form most of the knowledge of Mars through the 21st century. There was an issue with the corresponding part of the Viking I Lander sent to Mars. The boom latch pin in Viking I did not drop out of the scoop assembly as anticipated and caused the robotic arm to lock. Millions of miles away, NASA and contractor Martin Marietta engineers were able to troubleshoot the problem from the Lander’s transmitted images. They sent a set of commands to the spacecraft to extend the arm further, which freed the pin to drop to the Martian surface and allowed the mission to proceed with use of the important instrument. Now fifty years after the mission’s successful landing on Mars, the prototype sampler arm present here is a testament not only of exploration but human innovation and resolve in overcoming challenges millions of miles away.  Viking Program components, especially recognizable examples such as this, are extremely rare on the market.

title: STS-41B
description_block: THE FIRST UNTETHERED SPACEWALK  This striking photograph captures the first use of the Manned Maneuvering Unit (MMU) on a spacewalk, a propulsion unit designed to allow astronauts to perform spacewalks without a safety tether securing them near the spacecraft. Though successful, the unit was retired after its third mission; a safety review following the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster found the unit too risky.

title: T-38
description_block: A T-38 Talon Flight Simulator Panel Display The Northrop T-38 Talon is a supersonic jet designed for training Air Force, Navy, and NASA pilots. It was the world's first supersonic trainer aircraft. NASA added T-38s into their training program in the 1960s during Project Gemini. The T-38 spaceflight readiness training proved especially critical in honing skills used by astronauts during the shuttle program, both for those with military aviator training and for civilian mission specialists. This simulator panel dates from the 1980s and was produced for pilots in training to familiarize themselves with the flight systems and the order in which the systems are activated. An updated iteration of the aircraft is still in use by astronauts in training today.
